20003-the-infernal-marriage:
Disraeli's The Infernal Marriage is a satirical tale of gods and modern manners. It first appeared within his novel Henrietta Temple in 1837. Lady Ceres is promised to calm with time in its dialogue. What is done cannot be undone, the speaker soothes. A winter residence among the gods is even desirable, she is told. She may pay a visit by then, he predicts. Olympus here behaves like a London drawing room.

The tale retells Proserpine's marriage to Pluto as society comedy. Disraeli stuffs heaven with dowagers, dandies, and political talk. It is classical myth recut as a fashionable novel. Young Disraeli delighted in such blasphemous elegance. The piece shows his wit before Parliament tamed it. Readers meet the dandy-satirist in pure form.
20336-the-miraculous-revenge:
The Miraculous Revenge is a tale of Ireland, love, and a long-sought mystery. A man recalls first seeing a woman he hoped might solve his quest. On this night he watches and hears her only for that bygone hope. He applauds her generously as the curtain falls on her act.

Then he sups at a restaurant, returns to his hotel, and tries to read. Loneliness still sits with him despite the evening's bright show. Revenge in Irish tales often turns on wit, faith, and old wrongs. Readers get a moody, comic tale in the Irish storytelling vein.
20473-grace-harlowe-s-third-year-at-over:
In Grace Harlowe's Third Year at Overton College, published in 1914, Grace and her friends are deep into college life. The Eight Originals, as the friends call themselves, face a September parting. Miriam Nesbit and seven of the group spend a last evening on the Harlowes' wide veranda.

It is a warm night, and the talk turns on the day to come. The next morning will scatter the friends to their separate duties. The Grace Harlowe books followed their heroine year by year, and this volume catches the mix of freedom and farewell that college readers knew well.
20474-grace-harlowe-s-fourth-year-at-ove:
Grace Harlowe's Fourth Year at Overton College, published in 1914, brings Grace and the Eight Originals to their senior year. College rooms, parties, and old friendships crowd the chapters. Ruth and Grace plan one more gathering in a room they both know is too small.

Ruth remembers a Hallowe'en party in that same room the year before. It held eighteen girls one night, she says, and what a time they had squeezing in. The senior-year book closes Grace's college course with the warmth and loyalty that made the series a staple for girl readers.
20485-the-lunatic-at-large:
J. Storer Clouston's The Lunatic at Large is a comic novel that begins, as its title warns, with an escape. Its early pages introduce a young professional man in some detail. He may be described as amiable-looking, with a little fair moustache and still less chin.

He has no practice to speak of, and a considerable quantity of unpaid bills. A man of such features and in such circumstances, the narrator says, invites temptation. Clouston sends his characters through mistaken identities and absurd chases, in the brisk farce style that made this one of his best-loved books.
20667-a-canyon-voyage:
F. S. Dellenbaugh's A Canyon Voyage, published in 1908, narrates the second Powell expedition down the Colorado River in 1871 and 1872. Dellenbaugh went as a young artist and mapmaker. His book, written years later, is the fullest personal account of that voyage through the Grand Canyon country.

His figures give the canyon's scale. The gorge drops near six thousand feet on the north side and over five thousand on the south. Its total length, counting the Marble Canyon division, runs 283 miles. Dellenbaugh made sketches in colour on the spot, and the narrative keeps a painter's eye.
21197-diego-collado-s-grammar-of-the-jap:
Diego Collado, a Spanish Dominican missionary, published his grammar of Japanese in Latin in 1632, one of the earliest European studies of the language. Richard L. Spear edited and translated it for the University of Kansas East Asian series. His introduction compares Collado's account with the grammar by João Rodrigues.

Spear explains Collado's framework for Japanese sounds, word forms, and sentence structure before the translation begins. The 1632 original, Ars Grammaticae Iaponicae Linguae, also circulates as a separate text. For students of language history, the book shows how missionaries first fitted Japanese into Latin grammar terms, and where that fit strained. The book is old, rare, and hard to find in print now.
21405-the-loss-of-the-royal-george:
Ben Truscott's father was boatswain of the Royal George, and W. H. G. Kingston tells her loss through Ben's eyes. The great ship carried over a hundred brass guns and flew an admiral's flag. She had been launched in 1756 and was a pride of the navy.

Her sinking takes only a few pages, and the heart of the tale lies elsewhere. A small child brought aboard by a lady survives, while the lady drowns. A crewman raises the boy, who makes a good career at sea. In the last chapter his true parents are found, and all ends well.
21514-gryll-grange:
Thomas Love Peacock's Gryll Grange, his last novel, is shown here in the 1896 Macmillan edition. George Saintsbury writes the preface, and F. H. Townsend draws the pictures. Chapter heads promise squires, vicars, and a lord with a taste for grand dinners.

Peacock packs talk on science, exams, music, and the press into a country-house tale. A rustic lover, a thunderstorm, and the lottery of marriage stir the plot. Lord Curryfin's Siberian dinners and social tedium get sharp, funny treatment. The book is talk at its most sparkling, from a master of the comic dialogue novel.
21551-the-little-savage:
A boy grows up near alone on a rocky island in Captain Marryat's The Little Savage, published in 1848. His one companion, a morose and gloomy man, drags him over hard climbs and treats him unkindly. It was Marryat's twenty-sixth book, finished after his death by kin.

The tale was meant for children, and its religious tone sets it apart from Marryat's other works. Shipwreck, survival, and a child's slow schooling in faith and feeling drive the plot. Marryat died the year it appeared, leaving the book as a gentler last word. Its island scenes still hold young readers fast.
21639-when-patty-went-to-college:
Jean Webster sends Patty to a women's college in When Patty Went to College, published in 1903. Patty's roommate Priscilla drags pillows and curtains from a dry-goods box at term's start. Fifty girls, Patty jokes, have already begged the janitor Peters for his hammer.

Chapters treat an early fright, a question of ethics, and the elusive Kate Ferris. Patty comforts friends, pursues old English, and meets a bishop with grace. C. D. Williams draws the pictures, from Patty's portrait onward. Webster later won fame with Daddy-Long-Legs, and her wit and warmth are already here in full.
21701-the-settler-and-the-savage:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote adventure novels for young readers in the nineteenth century, and this one is set in South Africa. The story opens on the great dry plains called the karroo in the first quarter of that century. A young rider named Charlie Considine is lost there with his horse, Rob Roy, short of water under a hot sun.

From that hard start, the tale follows Charlie among settlers and the wild country around them. Ballantyne had a gift for plain, fast storytelling, and he fills the pages with travel, danger, and close escapes. Readers get a vivid picture of frontier life in southern Africa as English settlers saw it, told as a boy's own adventure.
21866-the-gundungurra-language:
An Australian Aboriginal language is set down on paper in R. H. Mathews's study of Gundungurra, read before a learned society in October 1901. The Gundungurra and Dharrook peoples held country from the Hawkesbury River to Mount Victoria and south to Berrima and Goulburn. Mathews notes features not before reported in Australia. Nouns, verbs, and pronouns carry rich inflections, and the first person has two forms each of dual and plural.

He spells every word phonetically in nineteen English letters and explains each sound. The little word for yes, ngee, opens his notes on the tricky ng. Such papers, dry as they look, preserve languages under heavy pressure. Mathews's record remains a source for Gundungurra descendants and linguists alike.
21995-philosophy-and-religion-six-lectur:
Materialism is impossible, argues Hastings Rashdall in Philosophy and Religion, six lectures delivered at Cambridge and published in 1909. Rashdall, fellow of New College, Oxford, begins with mind and matter. All we know of matter, he says, implies mind: color and sound plainly, but solidity and size no less. This was Berkeley's great discovery, though Berkeley blurred parts of it.

If matter cannot exist apart from mind, Rashdall reasons, there must be a universal mind in which all things exist: God. Yet he grants that theism is possible without idealism. The lectures move with a tutor's patience from Spinoza and Spencer to faith. They show Edwardian Oxford philosophy at its clearest, arguing for religion on reason's own ground.
22001-pastoral-poems-by-nicholas-breton-:
Three Elizabethan pastoral poets share this slim booklet of 1906, third in the Pembroke Booklets series from Hull. Nicholas Breton (1558 to 1626) leads with his pastoral poems; Ben Jonson praised his work as the habit of true passion in perfect strains. George Wither (1588 to 1667) follows with selected poetry. Charles Lamb's praise heads his section: Wither first found poetry a present wealth, not only a hope after death.

William Browne of Tavistock closes the volume with his pastoral poetry. The editor warns that the fate of poets is uncertain, and these three survive but slowly in public interest. The edition was limited to two hundred fifty large-paper copies. It is a small act of rescue for the singing shepherds of England's golden age of verse.
22183-wilton-school-or-harry-campbell-s-:
Wilton School; or, Harry Campbell's Revenge is a school story told as a tale. It opens on a sad summer evening in a little farm by Wilton church. The low, dim parlour, panelled in oak, looks across the quiet churchyard. Lindens shade the gravel path, and sorrow sits inside despite the sweet weather without.

From that farm the tale sends Harry Campbell to Wilton School. Schoolboy honour, injury, and the hunger for revenge drive the plot. The book belongs to the early school-story kind, before the genre found its classic shape. Its moral is worked out through friendship and disgrace rather than games, which came later to rule such fiction.
22244-miss-pat-at-artemis-lodge:
Pemberton Ginther wrote Miss Pat at Artemis Lodge in 1917, one of her Miss Pat books for girls. Patricia and her friends have settled at Artemis Lodge, an art colony. The story opens in a flurry: the train is in, and Judith begs Elinor to watch one corner while she watches the other. Bruce has gone for a taxi so as not to lose a minute, and a beloved arrival is expected any second.

Studies, models, pranks, and friendships fill the girls' days at the lodge. Ginther writes bright boarding-house comedy with art-school trimmings. The Miss Pat series followed its heroine from school to art study and beyond. This volume shows the series at its sunniest.
22845-the-beauty-of-the-village:
One good workman carries The Beauty of the Village, a character sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. Her subject is a man of the old school. He served his employers faithfully, never thought his work beneath him, and filled every family role with credit. A big family grew up well under his care. Drink never drew him into a tavern once.

Mitford's title plays gently against expectations. The village beauty here is not a face but a life. Through one man's steady record she praises the unnoticed virtues that hold a parish together. The sketch is brief, warm, and exact. It shows why her village portraits were loved. She found the remarkable inside the ordinary and made readers see it too.
23242-laramie-holds-the-range:
Frank H. Spearman's Laramie Holds the Range, from 1921, is a western novel named for its hero. Its opening rides a train west. All day, a heavy train of sleeping cars has climbed the long rise from the river, across a dull stretch of treeless, short-grass plains.

Those plains run from the Missouri River to the mountains. Then the train stops again, almost without a sound. Spearman builds the West from such quiet details: distance, grass, and rail lines crossing empty country. Readers get a range story where the land itself sets the pace before Laramie takes hold of it.
a-crystal-age: W. H. Hudson's strange and lovely utopia pictures a far future of pastoral peace — no money, no strife, only gentle folk living close to nature. His dream of simplicity rebukes our hurried modern world. A beautiful, haunting vision from the author of Green Mansions.
a-straight-deal-or-the-ancient-grudge: Owen Wister's 1920 essays on America and Britain, arguing that the English-speaking peoples must stand together. Written after the First World War, they mix history, politics, and the Westerner's plain speaking. The author of The Virginian as public moralist.
alexander-s-bridge: Cather's 1912 Alexander's Bridge follows an engineer's divided heart. Ambition cracks. The Tower library holds the full text. It spanned ambition. Bridges rose. Hearts split. Tragedy fell. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
ammianus-marcellinus-roman-history-yonge:
Ammianus Marcellinus, a retired Roman officer, wrote his history of the empire in the late fourth century. C. D. Yonge translated the surviving books into English. Much of the full work is lost, but the remainder is rich.

The surviving books run from Constantius through the reign of Valens. Emperor Julian's Persian campaign receives a long, admiring account from a near witness. Ammianus writes with a soldier's eye for terrain, weather, and morale. Historians rank him as the last great historian of Rome. His pages remain a prime source for the late empire.
amours-de-voyage: Arthur Hugh Clough's 1858 verse novel: a young Englishman in Rome during the 1849 revolution falls in and out of love through letters in hexameter. Witty, skeptical, and modern, it is the great Victorian poem of indecision. A masterpiece too little read.
an-inland-voyage: Stevenson's account of canoeing through France and Belgium with a friend in 1876, sleeping in inns and camping along rivers. Written with high spirits and sharp comic observation, it captures the small pleasures of slow travel: good meals, strange fellow travelers, and rainy days in the boat. This early book shows the storyteller's voice that would later produce Treasure Island.
an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge: Bierce's 1890 Owl Creek Bridge hangs Peyton Farquhar in a dream of escape. Time stops. The Tower library holds the full text. It bridged Owl Creek. Rope tightened. Mind fled. Death came. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
at-large: At Large, E, w, hornung's raffles tale. The thief at large. This book preserves that story. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
birds-in-town-village: W. H. Hudson finds birds in town and village — the swifts, sparrows, and nightingales of English streets and lanes. His loving observations make familiar birds wonderful. A gentle classic of bird lore. Even London sparrows become marvelous under his patient eye.
by-conduct-and-courage: By Conduct and Courage, G, a, henty's tale, the brave conduct. This book preserves that adventure. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
by-shore-and-sedge: Bret Harte's California stories: "By Shore and Sedge" and other tales of the coast. Miners, gamblers, and golden-hearted outcasts in his inimitable style. The West as Harte imagined it, and America loved it. Harte's California made the West romantic for the whole world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-rene-le: A 1913 entry on Alain-René Le Sage — the French novelist of Gil Blas. Georges Bertrin sketches his satiric art. His lame devil lifted Parisian roofs. Comedy and moral kept company. France's beloved storyteller. His Turcaret mocked the financiers. His Diable boiteux exposed Parisian society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alger-of-lieg: This 1913 reference piece on Alger of Liège — the theologian of the Eucharist. John Joseph A'Becket notes his works. His De sacramentis defended the true Body. The schools remembered his logic. A schoolman of the twelfth century. His works rest in the old libraries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-hallows-c: This 1913 reference piece on All Hallows College — Dublin's missionary seminary. Thomas O'Donnell honors its world-wide work. Its priests carried faith to the ends of earth. Drumcondra trained a thousand missioners. Ireland's gift to the missions. Its alumni span five continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-ledge: A 1913 entry on the altar ledge — the gradine shelf behind the mensa. Augustin Schulte notes its practical use. Cross and candles stand upon it. Its step lifts the sacred vessels. The altar's handy shelf. Its width holds the missal stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarage: This 1913 reference article on altarage — the offerings that formed the priest's due. Augustin Schulte explains the old custom. The faithful's gifts fed the clergy. The practice shaped parish incomes. The altar's ancient revenue. Its abolition freed the parish priests. Its memory lives in the old glebes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-of-lie: This 1913 reference piece on Anselm of Liège — the chronicler of its bishops. Francis Grey notes his history. His pages lit the Meuse valley. The entry preserves his modest fame. A canon among chroniclers. His bishops fill the local annals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-josep: This 1913 reference piece on Antoine-Joseph Mège — a Maurist scholar of note. Michael Ott records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Benedictine press. A monk among the editors. His commentary served the choir monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-berlage: A 1913 entry on Anton Berlage — a theologian of the German schools. Joseph Selinger records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seminary. A teacher of the sacred science. His dogma served the Munster schools. His pupils filled the German pulpits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-col: This 1913 reference piece on the Apostolic College — the Twelve around their Master. Joseph Wilhelm tells their story. Christ chose them for the nations. The bishops descend from their line. The Church's first hierarchy. Their number was completed by Matthias. Their mission began at Pentecost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banns-of-marr: A 1913 entry on the banns of marriage — the thrice-called proclamation. Thomas Shahan explains their prudent use. The parish hears the coming union. Impediments are thus revealed. The Church's public notice of wedlock. Their proclamation is thrice repeated. Their reading precedes the wedding day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-age: A 1913 entry on the canonical age — the years the law requires. P.M.J. Rock sets out the solemn numbers. The priesthood asks twenty-four years. The bishop needs his thirty. The ages of the Church's offices. Its tonsure asks but seven years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carthage: This 1913 reference article on Carthage — the African primatial see. Maurice Hassett unfolds its glorious past. Cyprian ruled its great church. Augustine's Hippo was its suffragan. The Rome of the African Church. Its Byrsa hill crowns the ancient port.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dufre: This 1913 reference piece on Du Cange — the prince of the lexicographers. Paul Lejay honors his great Glossarium. His folios unlocked the medieval Latin. The scholars still mine his pages. The father of the Byzantine studies. His Historia Byzantina is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b: This 1913 reference piece on Cardinal Bainbridge — the Archbishop of York. Henry Birt honors his Roman embassy. He died by poison in the holy city. The sacred college mourned its English son. A prince of the Tudor Church. His Rome tomb is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cities-of-ref: A 1913 entry on the cities of refuge — the manslayer's sanctuary. James F. Driscoll unfolds their merciful law. The avenger waited at the gates. The high priest's death freed the exile. The mercy of the Mosaic law. Their six cities dotted the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-marriag: A 1913 entry on civil marriage — the state's wedding contract. Walter George Smith sets out its legal bounds. The Church guards the sacramental bond. The faithful need the priest's blessing. The jurisprudence of the marriage tie. Its Napoleonic code is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college: This 1913 reference article on the college — the school of higher learning. Robert Schwickerath surveys its historic rise. The medieval halls bred the scholars. The Church mothered the learned arts. The cradle of the university's youth. Its quadrangle is the scholars' home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concubinage: A 1913 entry on concubinage — the illicit union's moral judgment. H.A. Gaynor unfolds the Church's law. The sacrament alone makes the marriage. The canons punish the scandalous bond. The ethics of the unlawful union. Its Trent canons are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-o: This 1913 reference piece on the councils of Orange — the Gallic synods. Nicholas Weber honors their famous canons. The second Orange crowned the grace debate. The sixth century dates their solemn acts. The synods of the southern city. Their 529 canons are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deluge: A 1913 entry on the Deluge — the Flood's scriptural tale. Anthony Maas unfolds its famous history. Noah's ark rode the destroying waves. The dove brought the olive's leaf. The judgment of the ancient world. Its Ararat landing is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demiurge: This 1913 reference article on the demiurge — the Gnostics' world-maker. John Arendzen unfolds its curious doctrine. The lesser god shaped the flawed world. The schools rejected the base fancy. The artisan of the heretical systems. His Ialdabaoth is the Gnostics' name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica: This 1913 reference piece on the ecclesiastical judge — the tribunal's president. Johannes Baptist Sägmüller unfolds his solemn office. He weighs the proofs with prudent care. The sentence binds the willing litigants. The magistrate of the Church's courts. His officialis is the canonists' term.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-james-c: This 1913 reference article on Coleridge — the Jesuit writer. John Gerard honors his famous works. His pen served the English province. The order prized its learned son. A father among the editors. His 1893 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ma: A 1913 entry on marriage's history — the wedded bond. John Augustine Ryan unfolds its sacred laws. The Church guards the holy union. The ages kept the seemly rite. The story of the Christian home. Its 1919 manuals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-lamy-b: A 1913 entry on Besange — a French writer of note. John Corbett lists his works. Little is known of his career. The seventeenth century was his period. The learned press knew his pen. His 1690 works are famed. His 1690 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lafarge: This 1913 reference piece on Lafarge — the American artist. John Lafarge recounts his famous works. His brush graced the storied churches. The age prized the gifted hand. The windows keep his art. His 1910 death is famed. His 1910 windows are famed. His 1910 church windows are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kimberley-in-: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Kimberley in Orange — the South African diocese. Armand Langouet gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the diamond-field flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the southern veld. Its 1910 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knowledge: This 1913 reference piece on Knowledge — the philosophical act. Charles Dubray unfolds its scholastic lore. The mind grasps the thing's form. The schools prized the seemly bounds. The philosophers weigh its kinds. Its 1907 study is famed. Its scholastic form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liberatus-of-: This 1913 reference article on Liberatus — the Carthaginian deacon. Adrian Fortescue honors his famous Breviarium. His pen recorded the Three Chapters. The East prized the learned name. The sixth century knew his toil. His 566 death is famed. His 566 Breviarium is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liege: This 1913 reference piece on Liège — the Belgian diocese. Joseph Brassinne gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Meuse flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Walloon land. Its 4th-century see is famed. Its prince-bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liguge: This 1913 reference article on Ligugé — the Poitevin abbey. Gilbert Huddleston gives its storied past. Its monks guard the ancient church. The ages bless the holy house. The Clain guards its walls. Its 361 founding is famed. Its Martin's cell is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-henri-d: This 1913 reference piece on Lestrange — the Trappist reformer. Marie Gildas honors his austere rule. His zeal restored the Cistercian rigor. The order bless the steadfast name. The nineteenth century knew his sway. His 1827 death is famed. His 1827 rigor is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuterge: This 1913 reference article on the Manuterge — the Mass towel. Joseph Braun unfolds its liturgical lore. It dries the priestly hands. The Church keeps the ancient use. The sacristies know its form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its linen form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maynooth-coll: This 1913 reference piece on Maynooth — the Irish seminary. John Hogan unfolds its founding tale. It schooled the Erin's priests. The isle bless the learned halls. The nineteenth century knew its name. Its 1795 founding is famed. Its priestly halls are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mixed-marriag: A 1913 entry on Mixed Marriage — the divided union. William Fanning unfolds its canonical lore. It weds the differing faiths. The canonists weigh the seemly bounds. The Church keeps its ancient rule. Its 1907 study is famed. Its cautious rule is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-and-can: Marriage is both a sacrament and a contract, and this entry examines it from both sides: its moral ends, its canonical form, and its indissolubility. The Church's full teaching on matrimony, systematically laid out, from consent to indissolubility, with the canon law of impediments explained.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-st-mary: Mount St. Mary's in Emmitsburg, Maryland, is one of America's oldest Catholic seminaries, founded in 1808 amid the Catoctin Mountains. This entry covers its foundation, its schools, and its place in American Catholic education. The cradle of the American priesthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-marr: Mystical marriage is the soul's highest union with God, described by the saints as a spiritual betrothal. This entry explains the concept, its stages, and its witnesses from Catherine to Teresa. The soul as bride: the Song of Songs gave the mystics their language of union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-hall-st-e: Old Hall, or St. Edmund's College, was the great English seminary that trained priests through the penal years and beyond. This entry traces its history, its presidents, and its alumni. The nursery of the English clergy: its alumni served every English county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-st-: This entry surveys the orders of chivalry under St. George's patronage across Europe, tracing their foundations, their knights, and their histories as the 1913 editors recorded them. The dragon-slayer's many knights: their crosses flew from England to Russia and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oscott-st-mar: Oscott, or St. Mary's College, was the great Midland seminary that trained England's priests after emancipation. This entry traces its history, its presidents, and its alumni. The seminary of the Midlands: its alumni rebuilt English Catholicism in the Victorian age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patron-and-pa: Patronage is the founder's right of presenting to a benefice, and this entry explains its history, its law, and its kinds. The founder's lasting voice in the church he built: the entry traces its long history from Rome to Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perge: Perge was the Pamphylian city where Paul preached on his first missionary journey. This entry covers its bishops, its ruins, and its apostolic fame. The city of Paul's first voyage: its vast theater is counted among the finest in Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privilege: Privilege is the law's favor granted to a person or place. This entry explains its kinds, its acquisition, and its loss. The exception that proves the rule: its gracious grants favor the worthy petitioner in honest need and humble faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-putative-marr: A putative marriage is the union believed valid though canonically flawed. This entry explains its effects, its children, and its law. The marriage of good faith: its innocent children are legitimate in law and in Church courts alike in justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritual-of-mar: The ritual of marriage is the Church's wedding rite. This entry explains its prayers, its customs, and its law. The blessing of the nuptial Mass: its solemn vows bind the pair for life in Christ Jesus our Lord and King.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatine-pri: The Sabbatine Privilege is the Carmelite promise of Mary's aid. This entry examines its bull, its meaning, and its devotion. The Saturday freedom of the scapular: its Marian promise aids the wearer of Carmel's scapular in death's hour of need.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrament-of-: The sacrament of marriage is the union of the baptized spouses. This long entry examines its institution, its effects, and its indissolubility. The bond of Christ and the Church: its holy grace sanctifies the Christian home in love and fidelity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrilege: Sacrilege is the violation of the sacred. This entry explains its kinds, its gravity, and its penalties. The sin against the holy things: its dark guilt profanes the sacred vessels of the altar in sin and shame and scandal and crime.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-eugeniu: St. Eugenius of Carthage was the bishop of the Vandal persecution. This entry notes his exile, his constancy, and his cult. The confessor of the African church: his long exile witnessed the faith in Sardinia's mines of the Vandals in the 480s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-selge: Selge, the Pisidian city of the Taurus, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Asia Minor: its ancient ruins crown the Taurus in Pisidia's mountains in the range.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ou: The Sisters of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge are the daughters of Caen. This entry covers their rule, their penitents, and their houses. The sisters of St. John Eudes: their rescued penitents fill the refuges in the 1640s.

cicero-de-natura-deorum-yonge:
Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, written in 45 BC, stages a debate on religion among Rome's educated elite. C. D. Yonge's translation, from the Harper edition of 1877, is the text here. Cicero sets the scene at a friend's villa and mostly listens.

An Epicurean speaker argues the gods exist but care nothing for human affairs. A Stoic answers that divine reason runs the world and watches over it. An Academic skeptic then takes both cases apart, finding each one wanting. The dialogue is the fullest surviving survey of ancient thought on the gods, and its balance made it a school text for centuries.
cicero-philippics-yonge:
Cicero's Philippics are fourteen speeches against Mark Antony, delivered in 44 and 43 BC after the murder of Julius Caesar. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here, drawn from the fourth volume of his Orations. Cicero named them after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon.

An old man with no army, Cicero used speech alone to brand Antony a public enemy and rally the Senate against him. The gamble worked for a season, then failed: the triumvirs proscribed him, and Antony had him killed in December 43 BC. The speeches are his last stand for the republic. They cost him his life and fixed his fame.
cicero-tusculan-disputations-yonge:
Cicero wrote the Tusculan Disputations in 45 BC at his villa in Tusculum, in the last stretch of his career. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here. The work holds five days of talk with friends on how to face life's hardest blows.

Each day takes one fear: death, pain, grief, the passions of the soul, and the question whether virtue alone makes a happy life. Cicero argues death is no evil, pain can be borne, and grief yields to reason. His answers lean Stoic, though he keeps his Academic freedom to doubt. The talks became a handbook of calm for later ages.
diary-of-a-pilgrimage: Jerome's 1891 comic travelogue about a pilgrimage to Oberammergau to see the Passion Play. Funny, digressive, and full of his cheerful philosophy, it is Jerome abroad at his best. Delightful Victorian humor. Jerome on tour is Jerome at his funniest and most good-natured.

english-men-of-letters-coleridge: H. D. Traill profiles Samuel Taylor Coleridge — poet of the Ancient Mariner, philosopher, and opium-haunted genius — for the English Men of Letters series. Sympathetic and acute, the study captures both the glory and the tragedy. A fine short biography of a complex great man.
faxian-record-buddhistic-kingdoms-legge:
Faxian, a Chinese Buddhist monk, recorded his pilgrimage to India in 414 CE. James Legge translated the Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms into English. Faxian had walked from China through Central Asia between 399 and 414.

He crossed deserts and mountains seeking complete texts of monastic rules. Kingdoms, monasteries, and relics of the Buddha fill his spare narrative. Storms at sea nearly ended his return voyage with his books. The record is the earliest surviving Chinese travel narrative of its kind. Legge's translation trails him past countries now transformed or gone. Adventure and devotion combine in Faxian's calm, factual voice throughout.
framley-parsonage: Anthony Trollope's 1861 Framley Parsonage: Mark Robarts's debts and Lucy's love. The fourth Barsetshire novel, warm and wise. Trollope at his most readable. A parson's debts and a lady's love, trollope's Barsetshire at its best, Trollope's Barsetshire at its very best.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BernauGeorgePro: Gary Hart, the Colorado senator with a lifelong interest in the Kennedy era, is the reviewer in this file: his subject is 'Promises to Keep' by George Bernau. The document preserves the review as released, a senator's published judgment on a book from the Kennedy literature that fills this archive. It is kept as issued, one of the many press pieces gathered by the researchers who collected everything the case produced in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ColumbiaCollege:
In April 1970 Harold Weisberg quarreled by mail with Mirron Alexandroff, president of Columbia College in Chicago. The subject was Sherman Skolnick, the Chicago researcher, whom Weisberg accused of plagiarizing his materials in a federal court filing.

Skolnick taught and broadcast in Chicago and drew on the case's literature freely, and Weisberg guarded his documents with famous jealousy. The letters show the movement's internal policing: credit and theft argued out, with a college president drawn into the exchange. It sits in Weisberg's files as an unusually formal record of a researchers' feud, argued on letterheads.

govdocs-archive_org-ragnarokkr-parts-i-i: Ragnarøkkr, Parts I and II, presents itself as a strategic alert on hybrid warfare, dated August 2025. Hybrid warfare mixes soldiers, hackers, propaganda, and crime against a target state. The library holds the work as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. grace-harlowe-s-second-year-at-overton-c: Josephine Chase follows Grace Harlowe through her sophomore year at Overton College — new friendships, college pranks, and the small tests of character that shape young women. The Grace Harlowe books were beloved by generations of schoolgirls. Wholesome, spirited college life as readers once dreamed it.
hofmannsthal-der-schwierige:
Hans Karl, an aristocrat so sensitive and scrupulous that ordinary social life defeats him, carries Hofmannsthal's comedy Der Schwierige, given here in German. The Difficult Man sparkles with dialogue set in a Vienna of salons and matchmakers after the Great War. Everyone wants Hans Karl married; Hans Karl can barely finish a sentence at a party.

Love finds a way through the glittering talk, as tact and feeling slowly align. Hofmannsthal turns social embarrassment into high comedy without a cruel line anywhere. The play is often called the wittiest Austrian comedy of the twentieth century. Its humane wisdom hides inside perfect manners. German readers who relish language itself will be in their element here.
hsiao-king-legge:
James Legge translated the Hsiao King, the Classic of Filial Piety, for the Sacred Books series. Tradition links the short text to Confucius and his disciple Zengzi. Legge's version appeared within the third volume of the Sacred Books of the East.

The text holds that care for parents roots all virtue and sound rule. A dialogue between Confucius and Zengzi unfolds the doctrine by degrees. Filial piety extends from serving parents to serving rulers and Heaven. Emperors promoted the book across East Asia for two thousand years. Schoolchildren memorized its chapters as a first moral textbook. Small in size, the Hsiao King carried enormous sway over family and state alike.
in-the-bishop-s-carriage: This novel follows adventures in a bishop's carriage across country. The road reveals character gradually. The Tower library holds the full text. It journeyed by carriage slowly. Passengers shared stories freely. The miles taught lasting lessons. Readers enjoyed the pleasant ride.
in-the-cage: Henry James's 1898 novella about a telegraph girl in a London post office who becomes entangled in the romances of her wealthy customers. Through her sharp, lonely imagination, James studies class, longing, and the stories we invent. Subtle and quietly heartbreaking.
ladysmith-the-diary-of-a-siege:
H. W. Nevinson kept this diary during the siege of Ladysmith in the Boer War. Methuen published it in London in 1900. Nevinson had already written about a thirty days' war.

Early chapters cover the war's first week and the battle of Elandslaagte. A reverse at Nicholson's Nek follows, then the town is hemmed in. Nevinson records tragedy, comedy, and sudden death side by side. Signals from General Buller flash into the later chapters. His diary gives a ground-level record of a famous siege. Daily entries keep the fear and boredom of siege life vivid. Nevinson writes as a witness, not a distant historian.
life-and-gabriella-the-story-of-a-woman-:
Ellen Glasgow published this novel with Doubleday, Page in 1916. Its heroine is Gabriella, whose story the subtitle calls a woman's courage. Two large parts divide her life into an Age of Faith and an Age of Knowledge. Chapter titles trace her path from faith through disenchantment to success.

Gabriella starts life, meets motherhood, and then makes a second start. Work, discoveries, and readjustments fill her later chapters. The final chapters test her and weigh dream against reality. Glasgow builds a full portrait of a woman remaking her own life. Garden City, New York, was the home of its publisher that year.
marriage:
Marriage is a novel by H. G. Wells, dated 1912. Duffield published it at New York among his social novels. A motto from a private letter sets its ironic key. 'The Poor Dears haven't the shadow of a doubt they will live happily ever afterwards.'

Wells follows a young couple into the real business of marriage. Love meets money, work, and the problem of a useful life. His hero is a scientist drawn toward big business and its millions. His heroine must weigh comfort against her husband's soul. Wells writes marriage as the central adventure of modern life. The novel argues, questions, and entertains all at once. It stands with his finest studies of Edwardian society.
matthew-westminster-flowers-vol-1-yonge:
Matthew of Westminster gathered the flowers of history in his great chronicle, Englished by C. D. Yonge in 1853. This first volume runs from creation through the Norman kings. Monks at Westminster picked the best tales from all earlier histories and wove them into one long story.

Saints, kings, battles, and wonders fill its medieval pages in turn. The Latin title means a bouquet, and the method shows on every leaf. English readers in Bohn's Library made it a favorite history book. The volume opens a window on how the Middle Ages themselves read the past: moral, marvelous, and utterly unembarrassed by legend.
matthew-westminster-flowers-vol-2-yonge:
Plantagenet kings rule in the second volume of the Flowers of History, in Yonge's 1853 version. Henry the Second, Richard the Lionheart, and King John pass in vivid review. Magna Carta is wrung from John by his barons, in the chronicle's own telling of the famous scene.

The great thirteenth-century chronicle shows England's past as its monks saw it. Moral judgment falls freely on good kings and bad alike. Feuds, crusades, and charters fill the long annals year by year. The volume completes Yonge's rendering of medieval England's favorite history, a source still mined for the color and gossip that drier records leave out.
memoirs-of-arthur-hamilton-b-a-of-trinit:
Arthur Christopher Benson wrote the Memoirs of Arthur Hamilton, of Trinity College. The book first came out with no name in 1886. It draws on Hamilton's letters, diaries, and talks with his friend.

Christopher Carr, of the same college, is named as that friend. Benson's dedication treats a split in religious thought at the universities. He had seen both sides of that fight at close range. He hoped the book might help heal a breach more of words than of fact. Latin lines from Juvenal head the dedication in this copy. Benson gave the book to a friend who shaped his own views.
murder-at-bridge:
Anne Austin wrote this mystery novel, issued in February 1931. It was reprinted three times within a year. Austin had written Murder Backstairs before it. A floor plan shows the house in Primrose Meadows, and the room of the crime.

Chapter one meets Bonnie Dundee, a cheerful young detective type. He lounges in an office chair that is not his. Miss Crain, at her typewriter, snaps back at his ease. Their sparring sets a light tone before the killing. The bridge table gives the case its hook, a murder tied to cards, guests, and a neat country house.
nasa-tm-19650019848-automatic-recording-:
Paul A Faeth at Lewis Research Center described a modified McLeod gauge in a paper prepared in July 1964. A McLeod gauge measures very low gas pressures, the near-vacuum range. Vacuum work was central to space testing, from chambers that mimic orbit to studies of thin gases. Faeth's change lets the gauge record pressure automatically.

Automatic recording frees a worker from reading the gauge by eye again and again. It also gives a continuous record that can be checked later. The paper was prepared for a journal of scientific instruments. Small instrument improvements like this one quietly raised the quality of vacuum data across many laboratories.
nasa-tm-19670006713-studies-of-low-and-h:
E. G. Zaretsky, H. W. Scibbe, and D. E. Brewe, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a lubrication conference in Miami Beach, Florida, in June 1967. It compares self-lubricating cage materials for ball bearings. The cage holds the balls in place, and its wear decides how long a bearing survives at extreme temperatures.

Seven retainer materials were tested in ball bearings spinning at 20,000 revolutions per minute in cold hydrogen gas under a heavy thrust load. Six high-temperature materials were also compared in a separate tester at 500 and 700 degrees Fahrenheit. Glass-filled and bronze-filled plastic cages laid down protective films and ran over ten hours with no race wear when cold. At high temperatures, two metal alloy materials wore least, and wear fell as material hardness rose.
nasa-tm-19690017165-sensitivity-of-subso:
Robert W. Koenig and Laurence H. Fishbach of Lewis Research Center calculate how engine design changes subsonic transport range in this April 1969 paper. The work supports NASA's Quiet Engine Program. A DC-8-61 type airplane served as the test case for the calculations.

Turbofan engines with varied turbine inlet temperatures, overall compressor pressure ratios, and bypass ratios were compared. Appropriate engine weight, size, and installation drag and weight values were used for each case. Two-spool and three-spool engines were both considered. No off-design analyses were made, the authors note. The results show which engine choices most strongly move transport range.
nicomachus-introduction-arithmetic-dooge:
Martin Luther D'Ooge translated Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic into English in 1926. Nicomachus of Gerasa wrote the handbook around 100 CE. It presents the Neo-Pythagorean number theory that dominated medieval mathematics.

Ratios, means, and the hidden traits of numbers fill its two books. Nicomachus classifies numbers as perfect, abundant, deficient, prime, and composite. Figurate numbers shaped like triangles and squares receive careful treatment. Boethius later carried this material into Latin for the medieval schools. Students learned arithmetic from Nicomachus's scheme for over a thousand years. D'Ooge's translation revived the number lore in modern English. Philosophy dressed as arithmetic describes the book's charm exactly. It reads with ease and charm to this day.
of-human-bondage:
William Somerset Maugham wrote the novel Of Human Bondage. The story follows Philip Carey from childhood onward. It opens on a gray day with Philip as a small child. His dying mother holds him and feels his feet. She notices the club foot that shapes his life.

Philip grows up shy, keen, and often unhappy. He searches for love, work, and a sense of purpose. It calls the book his search for meaning. The novel remains his best known long work of fiction. The opening scene sets the loss that marks his early years.
olaf-the-glorious-a-story-of-the-viking-:
Robert Leighton wrote this historical tale of the Viking Age. It opens with tax collector Sigurd Erikson in Esthonia. Sigurd rides to a port on the Gulf of Finland. There he sees a Norwegian dragon ship at anchor. A crowd watches a boy juggle knives nearby.

The boy is Olaf, skilled, well dressed, and bold. He tosses two knives and catches them with ease. Shipmen swear the feat cannot be beaten. The scene sets up Olaf's rise in a hard world. Leighton writes adventure grounded in northern sea life. Fine cloth and a gold neckband mark the boy's high birth.
on-the-advisableness-of-improving-natura:
Thomas Henry Huxley gave this address on science in 1866. He opens two hundred years earlier, in January 1666. London then rested between plague and the Great Fire. Defoe's History of the Plague Year pictured that terror. Fifty thousand Londoners had died in the plague months.

Huxley contrasts old explanations with new natural knowledge. People blamed God's judgment or man's malice then. Science offers tested causes and useful remedies instead. Huxley argues that knowledge should serve every citizen. His speech helped define the public role of science. By fall the Great Fire left five-sixths of the walled city ash. Rich folk who had fled the plague came back to their homes.
our-village:
Mary Russell Mitford's Our Village is a book of sketches of English country life. The contents of this 1893 Macmillan edition list them. Walks in the country come first. Then the first primrose, violeting, the copse, and the wood. Hannah Bint and the fall of the leaf close the set. They are small, exact pictures of a Berkshire village world, the work that made Mitford beloved.

Anne Thackeray Ritchie's introduction confesses she never met Mitford. She almost owes an apology for that lack, she feels. The sketches hold so vivid a presence. The voice rings like a chime of bells, with a hospitable, cheery greeting. For readers who are beginning to remember rather than look forward, she promises, no reading is more delightful.
overrompeling-eener-plantage:
Overrompeling eener plantage means the Surprise of a Plantation. It is an episode from the Dutch translation of Jules Verne's North and South. That is his novel of the American Civil War. Amsterdam issued it in the Wonderreizen series in 1887. Chapter one, aboard the steamboat Shannon, begins not with characters but with Verne's beloved geography lesson, here in Dutch.

Florida, he explains, is a long strip of land. It lies like an oversized splinter between the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico. Annexed to the federation in 1819, it shines only as a second-rank star. Its rivers run weakly over low ground, except the St. John; its soil is sandy and ringed with dunes; its people are thirds Spanish, American, and Seminole Indian. Verne builds his war story on that surveyed ground.
paul-prescott-s-charge:
Horatio Alger, Jr. presented Paul Prescott's Charge as the second volume of his Campaign Series. His preface states the idea plainly: every boy's life is a campaign, and success depends on integrity and steady duty. Paul battles adverse circumstances while holding to a charge received from his dying father.

The story opens in Wrenville with Squire Benjamin Newcome, the town's pompous justice of the peace and richest man. Paul's struggles against such settled power form the test of the book. Alger wrote it to encourage boys facing hard campaigns of their own.
podcast-tuckercarlson-PCFGuxUUKGE:
Episode five of Tucker Carlson's series The 9/11 Files traces how the attacks built the modern surveillance state. Titled From Tragedy to Tyranny, the chapter argues that fear after 9/11 let government claim powers it never gave back. Carlson hosts the dark survey himself.

The episode follows the laws, watchlists, and spy programs born in the attacks' wake. Carlson asks how a free country slid into tracking its own people. He argues each new crisis since has only widened the net. Questioning and vigilant viewers get the series' core claim about what the tragedy was used to build.
poems-of-coleridge:
Arthur Symons selected and arranged this volume of Coleridge's poems, adding an introduction and notes to guide the reader. Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote comparatively little poetry, but what he finished changed English literature, and Symons gathers the essential work in one place. The contents are a roll of wonders: the Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Christabel, and Kubla Khan stand at the head of the list.

Conversation poems and odes follow: Dejection, Frost at Midnight, the Nightingale, the Eolian Harp. This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison, the poem written from a garden while his friends walked the hills. Political odes on France and solitude in fear round out the selection. Symons, a critic of the symbolist generation, presents Coleridge as a modern master rather than a period piece, and his notes keep the strange, opium-haunted contexts in view.
preface-to-a-dictionary-of-the-english-l:
Samuel Johnson wrote this preface for his Dictionary of the English Language, the book that fixed English spelling and meaning for a century. He begins in humility and defiance at once. It is the fate of those who toil at the lower employments of life to be driven by fear of evil rather than attracted by prospect of good. Among these unhappy mortals is the writer of dictionaries. The pioneer doomed to remove rubbish from the paths of learning and genius without a smile.

Johnson recounts the survey that began the work: a language copious without order and energetic without rules. Wild exuberance resigned to the tyranny of time and fashion. He describes reading the writers, noting phrases, reducing the mass to method by rules that experience and analogy suggested. The preface became famous beyond the dictionary: the lexicographer can only hope, he writes, to escape reproach.
prudence-of-the-parsonage:
Ethel Hueston wrote a cheerful novel of a Methodist parsonage, copyrighted in 1915 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company and pictured by Arthur William Brown. The frontispiece shows a family upset over what Prudence put in the soup.

Chapters introduce Prudence and the rest of the family, then move through a ladies' aid meeting, a secret society, lessons in manners, hard winter economy, a burglar's visit, and coming romance. Hueston dedicates the book to her mother, who raised a whole parsonage full of lively young Methodists. Readers get warm comedy about faith, family, and small-town life.
red-pottage:
Mary Cholmondeley published this novel with Harper and Brothers in 1900, having already written The Danvers Jewels. An epigraph from George Meredith heads the first chapter: passions spin the plot, and men are betrayed by what is false within. The title itself comes from a line she prints: after the red pottage comes the exceeding bitter cry.

Chapter one opens with Hugh Scarlett riding in a hansom from a dinner in Portman Square. Like Sterne's starling, he feels a cage, though he sees no bars. He vows he will get out, as his thoughts run ahead to a house in Carlton House Terrace. Desire, duty, and social bonds plainly cage him.
revenge:
Robert Barr gathered twenty tales of revenge in this book, dedicated to James Samson, M.D. Their titles promise crime in many keys: An Alpine Divorce, Which Was the Murderer, and A Dynamite Explosion. An Electrical Slip, The Vengeance of the Dead, and Over the Stelvio Pass keep the threats coming.

Later tales include The Bromley Gibberts Story, A Modern Samson, and A Deal on 'Change. The Shadow of the Greenback and The Exposure of Lord Stansford add money and rank to the motives. Pictures show a safe blown open, a bomb launched into the night, and a blade wiped on a fallen man's clothes.
riders-of-the-purple-sage:
Zane Grey's western novel opens its contents with a chapter named for Lassiter, the rider who leads its cast. Cottonwoods, Amber Spring, and Deception Pass set the country, and The Masked Rider and The Mill-Wheel of Steers raise its dangers. The Daughter of Withersteen names the woman at its centre, Jane Withersteen.

Picture captions fill in the action: Venters and Bess share a meal on a terrace, Wrangle runs a race, and Oldring's knell is sounded. Surprise Valley, Black Star and Night, and the fall of Balancing Rock mark the late chapters. Love and Faith and Unfaith stand as chapter titles, naming the book's twin strains.
rudder-grange: Frank R. Stockton wrote Rudder Grange, a comic tale told in chapters whose headings all play on the phrase a novel style. Chapter I treats a novel style of dwelling-house, Chapter II a novel style of boarder, and Chapter III a novel style of girl. Later headings promise a novel style of burglar, then Pomona Produces a Partial Revolution in Rudder Grange, The New Rudder Grange, and a chapter on an unsuccessful broker and a dog. Pomona returns in Chapter VIII, and the list runs on from there.
sagard-grand-voyage:
Gabriel Sagard was a Recollect friar who spent a year among the Hurons. His Grand Voyage to the Huron Country first appeared in 1632 in French. Readers here meet the 1865 reprint of that early, vivid account.

Sagard describes Huron towns, food, travel, and faith with open wonder. His tone is naive, warm, and full of small daily detail. He writes as a guest who liked the people he lived with. The book stands as the first French account of Huronia in print. It keeps the Huron world bright and close, before disaster struck it.
shadows-of-the-stage:
William Winter gathered these papers on the stage with Macmillan in New York in 1893, from a copyright of 1892. A Shakespeare line about the best in this kind being but shadows fronts the book. Winter inscribed the volume to Henry Irving, in honor of all Irving had done to raise the stage.

Winter chose the pieces from hundreds he had written on drama across his career as a critic. Actors, plays, and great nights in the theatre fill the pages. Readers meet the American and English stage of the late nineteenth century through a critic who prized dignity, poetry, and high craft in acting.
signs-of-change:
William Morris delivered these seven lectures on social change on scattered occasions, gathered by Longmans in London in 1896. Morris, author of The Earthly Paradise, speaks openly as a socialist. Contents open with how men live now and how they might live, then turn to Whigs, democrats, and socialists.

Feudal England, the hopes of civilization, and the aims of art follow. The best-known lecture sets useful work against useless toil. Morris opens by defending the word revolution: a change in society's very basis, not mere riot. Craft, labor, and beauty join politics in his plea for a remade common life.
somebody-s-luggage:
A waiter tells the tale in Somebody's Luggage, drawn from the 1894 Chapman and Hall Christmas Stories edition. Chapter I is called His Leaving It Till Called For. The writer owns that he comes of a family of waiters, with five brothers who are all waiters and one sister who is a waitress. He gives his lines to Joseph, much-respected head waiter at the Slamjam Coffee-house in London.

He then takes pains to say what a waiter is not. The man who goes out to wait is not a waiter, nor is the extra hand called in at the Freemasons' Tavern, the London, or the Albion. Such hands may be got by the bushel for public dinners, known by their hard breathing and by taking the bottle half out. No man can lay down tailoring, shoe work, or shop work at will and take up waiting, he insists.
specimens-of-the-table-talk-of-samuel-ta:
Specimens of the Table Talk of Samuel Taylor Coleridge gathers the poet's talk at table. A kin visitor kept the notes. He gives the book to James Gillman of Highgate. Mrs. Gillman shares the gift page. The preface looks back near fifteen years. The writer then first came often into Coleridge's home circle. The force of his mind in live talk struck him at once.

On the first evening, the guest went home and wrote. He set down the chief heads of that talk. He used Coleridge's own words as well as he could. No plan to go on drove that first note. Vexation drove it. Such a strain of music should not die, he felt. The same feeling drew him back for years. His notes grew to a mass in that time. This book prints the parts fit for present reading.
tales-of-the-jazz-age: F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1922 collection captures the glitter and ache of his generation. The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, The Diamond as Big as the Ritz, and other stories mix fantasy, satire, and heartbreak. These are the tales that made Fitzgerald the voice of the Jazz Age — brilliant, restless, and already tinged with loss.
the-adventure-of-wisteria-lodge:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge as a Sherlock Holmes tale in two parts, The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles and The Tiger of San Pedro. Dr. Watson tells the tale from his notebook.

Watson dates the start to a bleak, windy day near the end of March in 1892, when a telegram came while they sat at lunch. Holmes stood by the fire in deep thought, then turned with a sly twinkle to ask how Watson would define the word grotesque. He argues the term hints at the tragic and the grim, not just the strange. Readers get a tale of a vanished host, a dead man's house, and a cruel exile from San Pedro.
the-ancient-irish-epic-tale-ta-in-bo-cu-: Front matter opens Joseph Dunn's English version of the Táin Bó Cúalnge, the Cualnge cattle-raid, printed in London by David Nutt in 1914. Dunn is a professor at the Catholic University in Washington. He is said to have done the tale entire into English for the first time. His sources were the Irish of the Book of Leinster and related copies. Two pages of the source are shown in facsimile. A caption quotes the old book: men of Erin and Alba shall hear Cuchulain's name.
the-awkward-age:
Henry James wrote a long preface recalling how his novel began from a small idea he hesitates to name. He says the work was planned in good faith for brevity, lightness, and simple comedy. Instead it grew far beyond that first plan.

James groups the novel with other works that started small and became, in his word, monsters. Fresh reading, he says, restored the flush of life to the pages and taught him a lesson from his own adventure. The preface is thus a study in how fiction expands. A grain of subject, given the right conditions, can cover far more ground than its author first meant.
the-bed-book-of-happiness-being-a-collig:
Harold Begbie gathered cheerful writings from many quarters into a book printed in 1914 by Hodder and Stoughton. A Charlotte Bronte line about a throng of glad faces stands at the front. Begbie calls the volume a friend to the invalid and a companion to the sleepless.

Verses to Sir Jesse Boot promise cheer for those who suffer, and a rondel says the book will stay beside the reader's bed, keeping cares away. Thanks are rendered to writers and publishers who lent pieces. The plan is plain: short, pleasant reading for tired or ill people who need distraction through the night.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-snow-lodge: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at Snow Lodge, with rights dated 1913 from Grosset and Dunlap. Its part names start with runaways, old Mr. Carford, a big snowball, and a charge laid. Then come the year-end break, a call on Mr. Carford, and the tale of Snow Lodge. A kind offer and Mr. Bobbsey's own tale lead to bad news, plans, and notes. The young folk then face a hard blow of snow on the way to the lodge, and a snow slide is named.
the-children-s-pilgrimage:
Mrs. L. T. Meade wrote this tale for young readers, opening in a poor part of London on an autumn Sunday evening. Two children sit side by side on a doorstep in a quiet cul-de-sac back of Bloomsbury. The elder, a girl of about ten, sits with her brother of about eight, and a mongrel dog lies before them with hungry, loving eyes.

The telling stresses that these are no East End waifs. They are clean and respectable in look, though their faces strike the narrator as foreign, unlike their plain English dress. The first part of the book is headed Looking for the Guide, under a hymn line about a dark night far from home. Meade thus sets two lost children on a search that is both a search across London and a matter of faith.
the-deluge: David Graham Phillips, author of The Cost and The Plum Tree, wrote The Deluge, with illustrations by George Gibbs. Its contents list thirty-six chapters. They center on a Mr. Blacklock and a woman named Anita: In Those Days Arose Kings, A Candidate for Respectability, Danger Signals, and Blacklock Goes into Training. A Genteel Hold-Up, A Conspiracy Against Anita, Wild Week, and Black Matt's Triumph close the list. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-english-gipsies-and-their-language:
Charles G. Leland's The English Gipsies and Their Language came out in a second edition from Trübner, dated 1874. Its preface rests on a firm claim. Every custom noted came straight from Gypsy mouths. So did every Romani word in its talks, tales, and sayings. Leland owns his debt to George Borrow yet says he repeats him in no detail, nor draws on Simson or Hoyland.

His pages give talks, tales, and word lists from the road. Leland, who wrote Hans Breitmann's Ballads, loved folk speech. The book stays a prime source on English Romani life and tongue.
the-golden-age:
Kenneth Grahame wrote The Golden Age. It is a set of tales and sketches of childhood. A contents list names The Olympians, A Holiday, and A White-Washed Uncle. It names The Finding of the Princess, Sawdust and Sin, and The Burglars. It also names Snowbound, The Argonauts, The Roman Road, and The Secret Drawer. A quote from Sir Thomas Browne stands at the front.

The prologue, The Olympians, looks back from grown life. The narrator recalls the days before the gate shut. Children kept by aunts and uncles saw the adult world in a special way. The grown folk met the needs of the flesh with kindness. Then they left the children alone. They were sure a child is merely an animal. Even as a small boy, he felt the weight of that adult error. It ruled the world around him.
the-golden-slipper-and-other-problems-fo:
Anna Katharine Green wrote The Golden Slipper and Other Problems for Violet Strange. She is also given as Mrs. Charles Rohlfs. A contents list names nine problems. They run from The Golden Slipper and The Second Bullet to Violet's Own. They name The Intangible Clew, The Grotto Spectre, and The House of Clocks. They name Missing: Page Thirteen.

Problem I opens at the opera. A man points out one of three young ladies in a box. She is here, he says. His friend turns his opera glass. He sees the Misses Pratt with Miss Violet Strange. He scoffs at the claim. The first man insists the belle is an agent. She solves problems in secret. The tales turn on that split: a society girl by day, a sharp detective by hire.
the-lifted-bandage:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews published her short novel with Scribner in New York in 1910. A man lets himself into his front door and staggers like a drunk across the hall. Still wearing his overcoat, he drops onto a divan in his library and stares through leaded window panes.

His butler Miller lights a fire, lowers shades, and asks gently about lunch. The man, addressed as Judge, can barely grasp the word. Andrews opens in a held breath of shock, letting servants care and a silent room tell readers that some blow has just fallen outside the door.
the-little-savage: Captain Marryat's adventure maroons a boy on a desert island, where he grows up wild — a savage by circumstance, not nature. His rescue and return to civilization test what upbringing really means. Exciting and thought-provoking, from the master of the sea story.
the-vital-message: Doyle's 1919 Vital Message argues spiritualism's truth. The dead speak. The Tower library holds the full text. It messaged vital. Seances held. Spirits came. Belief urged. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
their-pilgrimage: Charles Dudley Warner's Their Pilgrimage: American tourists abroad. The genial essayist's travel satire. A pleasant journey. American tourists in Warner's satire, a pleasant journey abroad, genial and shrewd, American tourists abroad, the genial essayist, travel satire.
un-un-res-united-nations-framework-conve:
Climate change got its founding treaty in the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. Nearly every state on Earth has since joined it. The text is a framework by design: it sets the goal and the rules of the road, and leaves hard targets to later deals.

The convention aims to keep greenhouse gases at a level that avoids dangerous harm to the climate. It asks rich states to lead on cuts and to fund action in poorer states. It also creates the yearly climate talks. Paris and Kyoto both grew from this root text.
voyages-in-search-of-the-north-west-pass: Richard Hakluyt gathered these tales of the search for the North-West Passage. Captains like Frobisher and Davis sailed into Arctic ice and fog. England hoped to find a short sea road to Asia. The voyages show the daring and the cost of that age.
